text.en: 1. Company profile

GPS stops at the door. ZaiNar computes position from the 5G and Wi-Fi radios already inside a building, synchronizing them to sub-nanosecond precision and locating any radio-emitting device to sub-meter accuracy with no new tags and no new anchors [S1, S2]. The buyers are hospitals, construction sites, factories and city agencies. The company is private, based in Belmont, California, founded in 2017, with roughly 50-60 employees [S4, S8]. The February 2026 round of $100M+ at a $1B+ post-money puts it on the late-stage, pre-IPO rung of the ladder [S1]. It is a software-track AI infrastructure company: it licenses software running over networks it does not own, so the decisive tests are license revenue, gross margin, and whether the capability gets absorbed into the wireless standard itself.
2. The round

The round is a growth, stealth-exit financing: $100M+ raised at a $1B+ post-money valuation — the price of the whole company immediately after the new cash lands — announced on 19 February 2026 [S1]. No exact raise amount, share price or post-money figure is published, so the stake bought per dollar and the dilution that follows cannot be derived from public sources [S1, S12]. No BSH vehicle or terms are on file (pipeline stage: sourcing), which leaves the disclosed mark itself as the thing to judge.

What that price already assumes cannot be measured the usual way. An entry multiple — the price divided by annual revenue — is undefined here, because no revenue, ARR or bookings figure exists in any source [S4, S9]. The only ratio available divides the $1,000M mark by the $450M+ aggregate of contracts and memoranda, giving 2.2x [C3], and that aggregate mixes signed contracts with non-binding letters of intent, so it measures the quality of a disclosure rather than the earnings power of a business. Measured against the one corroborated prior mark, the August 2021 Series A post-money of $579.37M, the new price is a 1.73x step-up over roughly 4.4 years, about 13% a year [C1] — the compounding of a decent credit fund, not of a breakout.
3. Investment highlights
ZaiNar's case rests on moat (12/18), market size and growth (9/12) and team and governance (6/10); it is thinnest on revenue growth and quality (4/15) and valuation (3/8).

items.en: Nine years of stealth produced a granted patent estate rather than a prototype, and that estate is what an acquirer would actually be buying. The company reports 100+ patent filings and 90+ issued patents with zero rejections, covering phase-based time synchronization and network-computed positioning, as of its 19 February 2026 launch [S1]. The claim is checkable in part: US10455350B2, a radiolocation asset-tracking method over a mesh network, is a public patent-office record naming the underlying approach [S14]. Co-founder and CTO Philip Kratz is the named inventor on the core positioning IP, which ties the technical asset to a person still in the seat [S5, S14].

Enterprises want indoor location and mostly still do not have it, and the category is compounding above 20% a year. The indoor location market — hardware, software and services that track people and assets inside buildings — is sized at $18.35B in 2026 rising to $50.10B by 2031, a 22.3% compound annual growth rate, by MarketsandMarkets [S10]. Healthcare, the lead vertical, grows faster still: $3.17B in 2026 to $13.83B by 2032, a 27.8% annual rate [S11]. An ABI Research survey found 87% of enterprises had not deployed a real-time location system, blaming cost, complexity and reliability, with 56% preferring 5G positioning — the gap ZaiNar's no-new-hardware model targets [S17].

The backers and the ecosystem seat are the kind that open carrier and silicon doors, which is the distribution this model needs. Steve Jurvetson of Future Ventures, who also sits on the SpaceX board, is the named director disclosed at launch, alongside advisor Andreas Weigend, former Chief Scientist at Amazon [S1]. Dealroom's round-by-round register shows SoftBank, Samsung, AME Cloud Ventures (Jerry Yang), Evolution VC Partners and Alchemist Accelerator among prior investors — silicon and carrier-adjacent capital, not only generalist funds [S8]. ZaiNar joined the Arm Total Design ecosystem for location awareness in physical AI, a silicon channel that sits alongside its direct enterprise sales motion [S16].

The scan below scores the eight things the decision turns on — how big the market is, how fast it grows, where the company ranks, what protects it, how it charges and whether it earns, how strong the team is, what the price assumes, and how it would ever be sold — each with the number behind it and where that number came from.

Market size and growth — 9/12, strong. The category is large and compounding above 20% a year, but no report sizes the software-only slice ZaiNar actually sells. The indoor location market — hardware, software and services for tracking people and assets inside buildings — is put at $18.35B in 2026 growing to $50.10B by 2031, a 22.3% compound annual growth rate, by MarketsandMarkets [S10]. Healthcare, the lead vertical, grows faster: $3.17B in 2026 to $13.83B by 2032, a 27.8% annual rate [S11]. Both totals include the tags and anchors ZaiNar's no-new-hardware model avoids selling, so the serviceable slice is smaller than either figure [C6].

Industry position — 8/15, adequate. A real technical position in precision positioning, held without a single named production customer to prove buyers choose it. Nine years after founding and seven months after the launch announcement, no named commercial customer appears in any source; Sacra states that as of August 2026 there were no named customers and no independent field benchmarks [S4]. The one named counterparty is the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, which selected ZaiNar as one of seven companies from 22 countries for a market-entry support program in April 2026 — access, not a production rollout [S3].

Moat — 12/18, adequate. The patent estate is the strongest asset in the file, and 3GPP standardization is the thing most likely to make it worth less. The company reports 100+ patent filings and 90+ issued patents with zero rejections in phase-based time synchronization and network-computed positioning, as of February 2026 [S1]; one of them, US10455350B2, is publicly viewable [S14]. Ericsson launched integrated 5G Advanced location services in January 2026 and demonstrated decimeter-level accuracy with MediaTek over a commercial network in August 2026, without proprietary middleware [S4] — the capability can arrive in the standard rather than be bought.

Revenue growth and quality — 4/15, weak. No revenue figure of any kind exists in the public record, so growth quality cannot be judged at all. → see Key risks. No revenue, ARR or bookings number appears in the launch release, the Tokyo announcement, or any press or vendor coverage reviewed [S1, S3, S4]. The registry's ~$24M ARR and +180% growth are self-labelled design-mock placeholders with no document behind them and are excluded here [S19]. The commercial aggregate moved from $450M+ in February 2026 to $500M+ in April 2026 [S1, S3], but no source separates binding backlog from memoranda of understanding, so the increase cannot be read as bookings [S4].

Business model and unit economics — 6/15, weak. The licensing model fits a software-track infrastructure company, but nothing about its economics has been disclosed. → see Key risks. The company charges through network software licenses, platform subscriptions, deployment and integration services and usage fees, sold via network qualification, then a paid pilot, then a production site license [S4]. That model survives a shift to carrier-native positioning only if the accuracy gap persists, because carriers would then resell it rather than replace it. Whether it makes money is not disclosed: no gross margin, EBITDA or burn figure exists in any source [S4, S9]. On the software track we would look for gross margin above 75%; getting there requires deployment and integration work to fall to a small share of contract value, and no evidence shows where it sits today.

Team and governance — 6/10, adequate. Technical leadership and the investor bench are genuine; the officer and board structure is thinner than a $1B+ company warrants. Steve Jurvetson of Future Ventures, who also sits on the SpaceX board, is the only named director [S1]; prior rounds drew SoftBank, Samsung, AME Cloud Ventures (Jerry Yang), Evolution VC Partners and Alchemist Accelerator [S8], and the company joined the Arm Total Design ecosystem [S16]. No CFO, controller or general counsel is named in any source for a company that raised $100M+ [S1, S4, S6, S15], and Forge and The Org list three co-founders — Alexander Hooshmand, Jake Levy and Eric Roselli — whom company communications never mention [S5, S15].

Valuation — 3/8, weak. The $1B+ mark has no revenue denominator, and the only corroborated prior mark makes the step-up look ordinary rather than exceptional. → see Key risks. The February 2026 post-money is $1B+ on a $100M+ raise [S1]. Against the corroborated August 2021 Series A post-money of $579.37M [S5, S6] that is a 1.73x step-up over roughly 4.4 years, about 13% a year [C1] — not the 64x-from-seed framing one aggregator's chart implies [S7]. Preqin's enterprise-value, revenue-multiple and EBITDA-multiple fields for this asset are blank [S9], and the aggregator comp set spans roughly 0.2x to 36x revenue across LiDAR, RFID and telematics businesses [S7] — too dispersed to settle a multiple [C5].

Exit certainty — 2/4, adequate. No IPO signal exists and the most plausible acquirers are the incumbents best placed to build the capability instead. Forge shows no confidential filing or S-1 activity and no available secondary price for ZaiNar as of 20 August 2026 [S5], so an exit realistically sits in 2029 or later and the position is illiquid until then. The strategic buyer list — Ericsson, Nokia, Cisco, HPE Aruba, Zebra — is the same set Sacra identifies as able to bundle competing positioning into existing infrastructure contracts at marginal cost [S4].

Risk-reward balance — 2/3, adequate. The downside is partly bounded by a real patent estate while the upside needs commercial proof that does not yet exist. The base case returns 1.26x over four years, about 6% a year [C8] — thin for a late-stage illiquid private position — against a bull case of 4.20x [C9] and a bear case of 0.28x [C7].

text.en: 4. Key risks

One risk carries everything else: nobody outside the company can tell how much of the $450M+ commercial headline is money the company will actually be paid. Every other judgment here — the price, the exit, the margin — waits on that answer.

items.en: Commercialization — The headline commercial figure cannot be read as revenue, because it blends signed contracts with non-binding memoranda and names no customer. The aggregate was $450M+ at the February 2026 launch and $500M+ by April 2026 [S1, S3], and no source anywhere splits binding backlog from letters of intent [S4]. Dividing the $1,000M mark by that $450M+ figure gives 2.2x [C3], which is not a valuation ratio at all — it is a mark divided by a number of unknown composition. What normal looks like matters here: a software-infrastructure company at this stage would ordinarily disclose ARR, and the absence of any revenue line nine years after founding and seven months after launch is itself the datum. For the risk not to bite, a large majority of the aggregate would have to be signed, priced and scheduled, and at least one production customer named. What to check: the split between executed contracts and memoranda, the revenue recognized to date, and the name of a single live production site. Impact: If the binding share is small, the bear case becomes the base case and the position returns 0.28x — a loss of roughly three quarters of the money even though the technology works [C7]. (9/10, High likelihood — because no source has produced a named customer or a revenue figure in the seven months since launch.)

Valuation & exit — The entry price has no denominator: a $1B+ mark sits on revenue that has never been disclosed. The base case assumes $200M of 2030 revenue at a 9x software-infrastructure multiple, or $1.8B, less 30% dilution to exit, giving $1.26B against a $1,000M entry — 1.26x, about 6% a year over four years [C8]. Judge that against what this type of company normally earns: infrastructure-software leaders trade at roughly 10-20x forward ARR when net revenue retention runs above 130%, so 9x is a conservative but fair assumption; the problem is not the multiple, it is that the price already consumes the growth. Pushing entry down to $800M turns the same exit into 1.6x, while $1.2B turns it into 1.1x — the entry mark, not the execution, decides this. For the risk not to bite, revenue would have to arrive well above $200M by 2030, or the entry would have to be struck materially below the February 2026 mark. What to check: audited revenue for 2025 and 2026, the exact post-money and share price, and whether any secondary trades below the round mark. Impact: The base case returns 1.26x over four years, about 6% a year [C8] — thin for an illiquid private position, and every point of multiple compression comes out of principal first. (9/10, High likelihood — because the mark is already set and no revenue exists to grow into it.)

Moat & defensibility — Standardization can absorb the product, because RAN-native positioning is already shipping and already accurate. Ericsson launched integrated 5G Advanced location services in January 2026 and demonstrated decimeter-level accuracy with MediaTek over a commercial network in August 2026, with no proprietary middleware in the path [S4]. The absorption test for this company type is blunt: assume the capability ships free in the next major release of the standard — what survives? What survives is the patent estate, 90+ issued filings in phase-based time synchronization [S1, S14], and that is a defensive-IP asset, not a revenue engine; the bear case values the whole company at $400M on exactly that basis, returning 0.28x [C7]. For the risk not to bite, ZaiNar's measured accuracy would have to stay meaningfully ahead of standardized positioning in real deployments, and its claims would have to hold up outside its own lab. What to check: an independent field benchmark against 5G Advanced positioning, a claim-scope review of the core patents against 3GPP Release 18/19, and whether any carrier licenses rather than replaces the software. Impact: If 3GPP Release 18/19 positioning becomes good enough, the patent estate is worth what an acquirer pays for defensive IP, which is the $400M bear exit rather than a revenue multiple [C7]. (8/10, Medium likelihood — because standardization is underway but the accuracy gap has not yet been measured by anyone independent.)

Commercialization — The economics of the business are invisible: pricing, gross margin and burn have never been published. The company sells network software licenses, platform subscriptions, deployment and integration services and usage fees, through network qualification, a paid pilot, then a production site license [S4], and no gross margin, EBITDA or burn figure exists in any source [S4, S9]. The rule this is measured against is the software track's: after delivery, customer-success and hosting costs, gross margin should exceed 75%, because that is what separates a licensing business from a systems-integration business wearing software pricing. An integration-heavy telecom sale can land far below that, and the 9x exit multiple in the base case is only available to a company on the right side of the line. For the risk not to bite, deployment and integration work would have to fall to a small share of contract value as sites repeat. What to check: gross margin by revenue line, the services share of each site license, and the current monthly burn against the $100M+ raised. Impact: An integration-heavy telecom sale can leave gross margin far below the 75% a software-track infrastructure company needs, which would break the 9x exit multiple the base case uses [C8]. (5/10, Medium likelihood — because the licensing model can reach software margins, but nothing disclosed shows it has.)

text.en: 5. Recommendation

body.en: Recommendation: pass on ZaiNar — a $1B+ mark carries no disclosed revenue, no named commercial customer nine years after founding, and a $450M+ headline that blends signed contracts with non-binding memoranda of understanding.

items.en: Entry: $1.0B+ post-money (February 2026), a rounded company-disclosed mark on a $100M+ raise [S1]. No BSH vehicle or terms are on file (pipeline stage: sourcing).

Fair value range: $0.6B - $1.3B, on priced-round precedent alone — the low end is the corroborated August 2021 Series A post-money of $579.37M [S5, S6], the high end adds 30% to the February 2026 mark for the new cash and the issued patent estate [C2].

Base case: 1.26x gross MOIC (money returned divided by money invested) and a 6% IRR (the annualized return) over a four-year hold, 2026 entry to a 2030 exit [C8]. Probability-weighted across all three cases the return is 1.5x [C11], and the cases below 1x carry 40% of the weight.

1. Company & key metrics

items.en: Nine years in stealth bought patents rather than customers. ZaiNar was founded in 2017 in Belmont, California, and opened a Tokyo office in April 2026; it stayed unannounced until 19 February 2026, when it disclosed a $100M+ raise at a $1B+ post-money valuation [S1, S3].

What it sells is software, not boxes — which is why the economics should look like infrastructure software if they are ever disclosed. The product synchronizes existing 5G and Wi-Fi radios to sub-nanosecond precision and computes the position of any radio-emitting device indoors, where GPS does not reach, with no new tags or anchors installed [S2].

The company charges in three steps, and each one is slow. Sales run through network qualification, then a paid pilot, then a production site license, billed as network software licenses, platform subscriptions, deployment and integration services and usage fees [S4].

About 85% of every dollar ZaiNar has ever raised arrived in one round in February 2026. Cumulative funding is roughly $117M across four rounds — $2M and $3M seeds in 2018, about $12M in the 2021 Series A, and $100M in February 2026 [C4].

text.en: What the snapshot means is simple and it is bad: the numbers that would let a buyer price this company are the ones that do not exist. Five of the seven standard operating lines — revenue, growth, gross margin, burn and runway — are blank, and they are blank across company disclosure, press coverage and three separate data vendors, seven months after the company chose to announce itself. What is disclosed instead is a patent count, a commercial aggregate that mixes contracts with memoranda, and a rounded valuation. Those are real facts about a real company, and none of them is a denominator. The one derivable ratio, 2.2x the $450M+ aggregate [C3], is weaker than it looks, because nothing establishes how much of that aggregate is binding.

text.en: The marks undercut this entry price rather than support it. The only corroborated prior mark is the August 2021 Series A at $579.37M post-money, confirmed by two independent vendors [S5, S6], and the step from there to $1B+ is 1.73x over roughly 4.4 years — about 13% a year [C1]. That is the compounding rate of a decent credit fund, achieved during the period in which the company says it built a 90-patent estate and a $450M+ commercial aggregate. One aggregator's chart frames the same history as 64x from seed by skipping the 2021 mark entirely [S7]; the interim mark is the honest comparison, and it makes the 2026 price look like a normal step rather than a validation of a breakout. Meanwhile the fields that would let an outside buyer check the price are empty in every direction: Preqin carries the February 2026 raise but leaves enterprise value, revenue multiple and EBITDA multiple blank [S9], no pre-money is published, and no secondary trade has printed. Pricing here means accepting a number the company chose and rounded.
3. Team & founder-market fit

items.en: Daniel Jacker — Co-founder and CEO. He held the company in stealth from 2017 to February 2026 and raised roughly $117M across four rounds on the way, including the $100M+ round that set the $1B+ mark [S1, C4]. What is verifiable is the capital raised and the nine years of runway he kept alive; what no source shows is an operating record — no prior company scaled, no revenue line he has carried before, and no enterprise sales organization he has built.

Philip Kratz — Co-founder and CTO. He is the named inventor on the core positioning IP, and the claim is independently checkable: US10455350B2, a method for radiolocation asset tracking over a mesh network, is a public patent-office record [S5, S14]. That is the one leadership fact in the file corroborated outside company communications, and it makes him the key person — the asset an acquirer would buy is the patent estate he authored [S1].

Steve Jurvetson — Director, Future Ventures. He is the only named board member anywhere, and he also sits on the SpaceX board [S1]. His backing is corroborated across every source reviewed rather than only company materials, and it is the kind of position that opens carrier and silicon doors; a multi-board venture director is also not a substitute for resident oversight.

Andreas Weigend — Advisor, former Chief Scientist at Amazon. Disclosed at launch alongside Jurvetson, and a verifiable public figure whose affiliation is consistent across company and independent sources [S1]. An advisory seat carries no duty and no authority.

Alexander Hooshmand, Jake Levy and Eric Roselli — listed as co-founders by outside sources, absent from the company's own. Forge Global names five founders, and The Org's chart lists Hooshmand as co-founder and board member, Levy as co-founder and COO, and Roselli as co-founder and head of defense and government [S5, S15]. None of the three appears in the February 2026 launch release or any later company communication [S1, S3]. Either the founding team narrowed without disclosure, or current officer roles are simply omitted; both readings are governance findings, and neither can be settled from public sources.

No CFO, controller or general counsel is named anywhere. Not in company materials, not in the launch release, not by Sacra, Tracxn, Dealroom, Forge or The Org [S1, S4, S6, S15]. A company that has raised $100M+ and carries a $450M+ commercial aggregate has nobody publicly identified as owning financial controls, reporting or the cap table.

text.en: Founder-market fit is proven on the technical side and asserted on the commercial one. Kratz's fit is demonstrated by prior work in the most literal sense available: the positioning method the business sells is a method he invented and the patent office granted, and the company reports 90+ issued patents with zero rejections in phase-based time synchronization and network-computed positioning [S1, S14]. Nine years of stealth that ended with a granted estate rather than a prototype is evidence that this team can build hard wireless systems. The commercial half of the fit has no such evidence behind it. Nothing in the record shows either founder has previously sold integration-heavy infrastructure software into hospitals, construction sites or carriers, and the go-to-market motion the business depends on — network qualification, then a paid pilot, then a production site license — is precisely the long enterprise sale that a first-time commercial team finds hardest [S4]. Seven months after the launch, with no named production customer and no signed carrier partnership, that gap is not yet closed [S3, S4].

The investor bench is the part of the governance picture that genuinely helps. Prior rounds drew SoftBank, Samsung, AME Cloud Ventures (Jerry Yang), Evolution VC Partners and Alchemist Accelerator [S8], and the company holds a seat in the Arm Total Design ecosystem for location awareness in physical AI [S16]. That is silicon and carrier-adjacent capital rather than only generalist money, and for a product that has to be qualified onto somebody else's network, who makes the introduction matters. It is worth being exact about what a register like that is and is not: Samsung and SoftBank on a cap table are distribution relationships in potential, not contracts, and no source attaches a committed volume or a contract value to the Arm seat [S16]. The unverified registry values that show Koch Disruptive Technologies and Foundation Capital as major holders are self-labelled design-mock placeholders with no document behind them, they do not appear in any third-party investor list, and they are excluded from every ownership statement here [S19, S8].

On governance the answer is that almost nobody can course-correct the founders. One named director oversees a company with no named CFO, no named general counsel, no auditor, no independent director and no filings on record — Tracxn's filings tab returns nothing at all [S6]. The consequence is concrete rather than abstract: the figures that carry this investment, the $450M+ aggregate and the patent counts, are unaudited claims with no external statement to check them against, so a data room would have nothing behind it to reconcile to. Nine years of stealth explains how a company arrives in this condition, and it does not change what the condition costs a minority investor. An option pool size, a liquidation-preference stack beyond the 2021 Series A's 1.0x non-participating preferred, and any protective provisions are all undisclosed [S5], so what a new dollar would actually buy in rights and in ownership is unknown. That is the governance fact that pairs with the price: a rounded mark, a blank denominator, and one director.

Weighed together, this is a genuine technical team inside an unfinished corporate structure. The bull reading is that a founder-inventor with 90+ granted patents and a Jurvetson-led register has the technical credibility and the introductions the model needs, and that finance and legal hires are ordinary post-stealth catch-up for a company that raised most of its capital seven months ago. The bear reading is that a $1B+ company with no locatable financial or legal officer and three co-founders its own communications never mention cannot demonstrate continuity or control to anyone outside it. The evidence favours the middle and leans bear on governance: the technical claim is corroborated by a patent office, and every governance claim rests on absence. This dimension scores 6 of 10.
1. Why this matters now

ZaiNar is an asset-light software business, and it has to be judged as one. Infrastructure companies in this layer fall into two families. Track A companies sell software and licences: they own no plant, their cost of goods is hosting and delivery labour, and the tests that matter are code depth, switching cost, gross margin above 75%, and how much last year's customers spend this year. Track B companies own the metal: racks, accelerators, dedicated networks, and the debt that paid for them, judged on utilisation, payback per unit of hardware and residual value. ZaiNar sits squarely in Track A. It ships no tags, no anchors and no base stations; it computes position from the 5G and Wi-Fi radios a building already runs, and charges through network software licences, platform subscriptions, deployment and integration services and usage fees [S4]. That choice is the whole investment. It gives the company the best gross-margin structure available in positioning and removes any hardware residual risk. It also means the company owns nothing physical when a network vendor decides to ship the same capability inside equipment the customer has already bought.

items.en: The buying problem is real and mostly unsolved, which is why a software-only answer gets a hearing at all. Indoor location is the set of systems that tell an operator where a person, a machine or a tool is inside a building, where satellite signal does not reach. An ABI Research survey found 87% of enterprises had not deployed a real-time location system, blaming cost, complexity and reliability, with 56% preferring 5G positioning over dedicated hardware [S17]. Those three complaints — cost, complexity, reliability — are precisely what installing a parallel network of battery tags and ceiling anchors creates, and precisely what a software layer over existing radios avoids. The survey is dated June 2021, so it sizes the frustration rather than today's purchase orders, and five years is long enough for some of that demand to have been met by other means.

The timing argument is that the radios finally got good enough, and the same fact is the central danger. Phase-based synchronisation across commodity 5G and Wi-Fi hardware is what makes sub-meter accuracy possible without new equipment, and ZaiNar spent nine years building and patenting it [S1]. But Ericsson launched integrated 5G Advanced location services in January 2026 and demonstrated decimeter-level accuracy with MediaTek over a commercial network in August 2026, with no proprietary middleware in the path [S4]. The window in which precision positioning is a product you buy rather than a feature that arrives with the network is open now and is not obviously open in 2031. An investor is paying for a window, not for a permanent position.

What nine years produced is a granted patent estate, and that is the asset an acquirer would be buying. The company reports 100+ filings and 90+ issued patents with zero rejections, covering phase-based time synchronization and network-computed positioning, as of its 19 February 2026 launch [S1]. The claim is checkable in part: US10455350B2, a radiolocation asset-tracking method over a mesh network, is a public patent-office record naming the underlying approach, and co-founder and CTO Philip Kratz is the named inventor [S5, S14]. What does not exist alongside it is commercial proof. Nine years after founding and seven months after the launch, no named commercial customer appears in any source, and no independent field benchmark of the accuracy claims has been published [S4].

text.en: So the question this section has to settle is not whether the technology works. It is whether a market exists that a software-only vendor can hold, and for how long. The entry mark is $1B+ post-money on a $100M+ raise announced 19 February 2026 [S1], with no revenue figure of any kind behind it [S4, S9]. When there is no denominator, the whole case has to be carried by the size of the opportunity and the durability of the position — which is why the market ceiling and the moat are argued here at length, and why a soft answer on either one is enough to decide the recommendation on its own.
2. Market & ceiling

We adopt MarketsandMarkets' indoor location market as the outer ceiling — $18.35B in 2026 growing to $50.10B by 2031, a 22.3% compound annual growth rate — and we adopt it knowing it is too generous [S10, C6]. A compound annual growth rate is the steady yearly rate that turns the first number into the last one; the arithmetic checks out, since $18.35B compounded at 22.3% for five years is $50.2B, within rounding of the published 2031 figure [C6]. We use this definition because it is the only sizing from a named research house that covers what ZaiNar's customers are actually buying: systems that locate people and assets inside buildings, across healthcare, industrial, construction and municipal sites. Its flaw is scope. The total counts BLE, UWB and RFID tags, ceiling anchors and the services to install them — the hardware a no-new-hardware software layer is built specifically not to sell [C6]. Every dollar of tag revenue inside that $50.10B is a dollar ZaiNar cannot address.

items.en: The broadest credible sizing is the indoor location market, and it is the one adopted here: $18.35B in 2026 to $50.10B by 2031, a 22.3% annual rate, from MarketsandMarkets, published June 2026. It counts hardware, software and services together across BLE, UWB, Wi-Fi and RFID [S10].

The lead vertical grows faster than the blend, which argues for healthcare as the wedge: MarketsandMarkets puts healthcare indoor location at $3.17B in 2026 rising to $13.83B by 2032, a 27.8% annual rate [S11]. Hospitals are where the operational pain — clinicians hunting for pumps and monitors — converts into a budget line most reliably, and it is the vertical ZaiNar names first.

The broader IoT pool bounds the spending positioning rides on, and it is not a ZaiNar market: MarketsandMarkets sizes overall IoT and digitisation at $547.06B in 2025 growing to $865.20B by 2030, a 9.6% annual rate [S11]. It is listed because narratives in this category reach for it; at roughly thirty times the indoor location total it measures a different thing entirely, and using it would overstate the opportunity by an order of magnitude.

A fourth set of figures circulates and cannot be relied on, which is itself evidence about how immature this sizing is. A single aggregator write-up, EntrepreneurLoop, cites two indoor-navigation projections in the same paragraph — $13.73B in 2024 rising to $39.62B by 2033, and $38.46B in 2025 rising to $783.23B by 2035 at 35.17% — naming no primary report for either [S13]. The two disagree by roughly twentyfold on the same nominal category. Neither anchors anything here, and the divergence is the reason we work from one named house rather than an average of available numbers.

title.en: Published market sizes: total indoor location versus the healthcare wedge

reading.en: Higher is better — but every bar includes tag and anchor hardware ZaiNar does not sell

caption.en: Healthcare is roughly a sixth of the category and grows faster than the blend, which is why the near-term case runs through hospitals rather than through category share; the taller bars are a ceiling that includes hardware, not a target [C6].

items.en: TAM — $50.10B in 2031, the full indoor location category including hardware and services [S10]. This is the outer wall of the room, not the part of it ZaiNar can occupy. It rests entirely on one research house's definition [C6].

SAM — Not disclosed, and not derivable: no published report isolates network-computed positioning software as its own category, so the software-only slice of the $18.35B 2026 pool is an assumption rather than a figure [C6]. Two deductions apply before any share is claimed. Tag, anchor and installation hardware comes out, because ZaiNar does not sell it. Then the room-and-zone accuracy that Cisco Spaces and HPE Aruba already expose inside wireless licences customers pay for anyway comes out, because that demand is met at zero incremental price [S4]. What remains is the precision-sensitive work — surgical-instrument and infusion-pump tracking, active construction sites, robot coordination on factory floors — and no one has sized it.

SOM — the only company figure that touches obtainable share is the commercial aggregate, $450M+ at the February 2026 launch restated as $500M+ in April 2026, and it is not revenue [S1, S3]. No source separates binding contracts from non-binding memoranda of understanding, and no customer is named [S4], so the increase cannot be read as bookings. Our own base case assumes $200M of 2030 revenue [C8] — under half the February aggregate, four years out — because a sale that runs network qualification, then a paid pilot, then a production site licence moves at that pace [S4].

text.en: So how big can this company get? On the evidence, the market caps ZaiNar nearer $20B than $100B, and well short of $500B. The reasoning is worth showing, because the gap between the headline and the ceiling is where most of the disagreement about this company lives. Start with $50.10B in 2031 [S10]. Remove the tag, anchor and installation hardware that the category counts and this model refuses to sell, and remove the room-level accuracy incumbents give away, and what is left is a fraction of the total that no report quantifies [C6]. A software vendor that took an implausibly dominant share of that remainder — enough to reach the $500M of 2030 revenue in our bull case — would be worth about $6.0B at the 12x revenue multiple we assume there [C9]. That is the top of the plausible range, not the middle of it. The single assumption that moves the whole picture is the hardware-versus-software split of the category: if the software and analytics layer is a third of the $50.10B rather than a tenth, the company's ceiling roughly triples, and nobody has published the number that would settle it. This is why the market grade is strong on growth and not on sizing.

No regulatory regime materially constrains this business today; the rule-making that matters is standards-setting rather than government, and 3GPP Release 18/19 work on native RAN positioning is argued below as a competitive threat rather than a compliance cost [S4].
3. Competition & moat

No one leads this market today, and in three to five years the likeliest leaders are the network equipment vendors rather than any positioning specialist. The datum is Ericsson: integrated 5G Advanced location services launched in January 2026, and decimeter-level accuracy demonstrated with MediaTek over a commercial network in August 2026 using standardised radio and chipset methods, with no proprietary middleware [S4]. Decimeter means about ten centimetres — close enough to the sub-meter accuracy ZaiNar sells that the distinction stops being a purchase decision for most workflows. When the company that supplies the radio can deliver the answer through the radio, the specialist is selling a second copy of something the customer already has a route to. That is the structural fact this section turns on, and it is the reason the moat grade is capped well below the quality of the underlying engineering.

title.en: Who ZaiNar actually competes with, and on what

rows.en: Network equipment vendors — Ericsson, Nokia

Positioning delivered inside the radio access network. Ericsson shipped integrated 5G Advanced location in January 2026 and demonstrated decimeter accuracy with MediaTek in August 2026; Nokia bundles positioning into Digital Automation Cloud and MX Industrial Edge private-wireless deals [S4].

The most dangerous group, because they are also the distribution ZaiNar needs. A carrier that can get positioning from its RAN supplier has little reason to license a third-party layer, and the same firms are the plausible acquirers [S4].
Enterprise Wi-Fi platforms — Cisco Spaces, HPE Aruba
Room-level and zone-level location exposed as a feature of wireless licence tiers the customer already pays for; Cisco added an asset-tracking tag in July 2026 [S4].

Removes the low end of the market from contention entirely. Every buyer whose workflow tolerates room-level accuracy is served at zero incremental cost, which narrows the contestable pool to precision-sensitive work [C6].
Dedicated real-time location vendors — Zebra, Quuppa, Humatics
Installed bases and channel reach: Zebra MotionWorks sells through partners in 100+ countries, and Quuppa's 2026 partnership with InPlay targets tag costs of one to two euros [S4].
Erodes the cost argument rather than the accuracy one. If a tag costs a euro, 'no new hardware' saves less than it did, and the pitch has to win on accuracy and deployment speed instead [S4].
Terrestrial PNT specialists — NextNav, Verizon Hyper Precise Location
NextNav runs a dedicated licensed-spectrum transmitter network with public-safety distribution and government testing credentials ZaiNar does not have [S4].

Adjacent rather than head-to-head: a different architecture chasing different contracts. It matters as a listed reference point for how the public market prices terrestrial positioning, not as a bidder on the same deals [S4].
3GPP standardisation itself
Release 18/19 work could absorb phase-based positioning into the carrier stack natively, making it a capability every compliant network ships [S4].
The bear case. If the standard becomes good enough, the patent estate is worth what an acquirer pays for defensive IP — the $400M bear exit rather than a revenue multiple, a 0.28x return [C7].

text.en: Read together, these five rows cut against the investment, and the reason is that they squeeze from opposite ends at once. Cisco and HPE take the low end by giving positioning away inside licences already sold. Ericsson and Nokia take the high end by building accuracy into the network itself. Quuppa's one-to-two-euro tags take the cost argument. What survives in the middle is genuine — precision workflows in hospitals, on construction sites and around industrial robots, where centimetres matter and a parallel anchor network is impractical — but it is a narrow band inside a $50.10B category, not the category [C6]. A standalone vendor in that band has real pricing power over a small pool. It does not have a path to owning indoor location.

ZaiNar coexists with the incumbents rather than replacing them, and that is the correct way to read every deployment claim. The software runs on top of 5G and Wi-Fi equipment that Ericsson, Nokia, Cisco or HPE sold, and it needs that equipment in place and qualified before a pilot can start [S4]. Nothing gets ripped out. The advantage of coexistence is that the sale is additive — no capital budget for new hardware, no forklift upgrade, a shorter approval path. The cost of coexistence is that the host controls the roof. The same vendors whose equipment ZaiNar depends on can ship the capability themselves, and a carrier partnership would put the company's software inside a network operator's commercial offer rather than beside it [S4]. That channel was described at the February 2026 launch as coming within weeks, and no source confirms one has been signed since [S1, S4]. Seven months of silence on the distribution that defines the model is the most informative absence in the file.

title.en: What actually defends this position, and what does not exist yet

rows.en: Patent estate — real, and the strongest asset in the file

100+ filings and 90+ issued patents with zero rejections in phase-based time synchronization and network-computed positioning, company-reported as of 19 February 2026 [S1]; US10455350B2 is a granted, publicly viewable record naming the approach, with CTO Philip Kratz as inventor [S5, S14].

Durable as an asset, uncertain as a barrier. Patents run to roughly twenty years from filing, so the estate outlives the hold. Whether the claims read on standard-essential positioning methods has never been reviewed independently, and that review is what would separate a licensing business from a defensive portfolio [S4].
Systems engineering depth — real, and hard to copy quickly
Nine years of stealth work produced sub-nanosecond synchronisation across commodity radios rather than a prototype, and the company sells sub-meter accuracy over networks it did not build [S1, S2].

Holds for two to three years against a new entrant, and not against Ericsson. An incumbent with RAN control reaches decimeter accuracy by a different route, which makes depth a lead rather than a wall [S4].
Accumulated site data — claimed, and the one that would matter most

The company argues that each deployment builds a persistent record of a site that makes the layer expensive to unplug, and reports tens of millions of dollars of contracts tied to that spatial data [S20, S4].

Unproven. Stateful data is what turns a positioning tool into infrastructure a customer cannot remove, but no named production site, no site count and no renewal data exists to show it is accumulating [S4].
Switching costs from deployment — absent as evidence
Not disclosed — no named customer, no contract duration, no renewal or expansion figure appears in any source [S4].
Cannot be assessed. On the software track we would test net dollar retention above 130%, and no figure of any kind exists to test [S4].
Distribution and channel lock — absent

Not disclosed — no signed carrier agreement has been announced since February 2026 [S1, S4]. Membership in the Arm Total Design ecosystem is a silicon channel signal with no contract value or committed volume attached [S16].
No lock exists today. Each enterprise is won one at a time through network qualification and a paid pilot, which is the pace that holds the base case to $200M of 2030 revenue [C8].
Brand and regulatory position — absent

Not disclosed — one named counterparty exists, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, which selected ZaiNar in April 2026 as one of seven companies from 22 countries for a market-entry support programme [S3].
Access, not a production rollout, and no contract value was disclosed. It opens a door in Japan; it does not defend a position anywhere [S3].

text.en: The pattern across the table is that the defensible things are technical and the absent things are commercial. Two moat sources are real and evidenced: the granted patent estate and the systems engineering behind it. One is claimed and would matter more than either if it were proven — accumulated site data that raises switching costs. Three are simply not there: retention, channel lock and brand. That mix is normal for a company that spent nine years in stealth. It is not normal for a company carrying a $1B+ mark, because a mark that size is usually paid for evidence that customers stay.

title.en: The moat is narrowing, and that decides the exit multiple

body.en: Two of the three forces acting on this position push the same way. Standardisation is advancing: Ericsson shipped integrated location in January 2026 and demonstrated decimeter accuracy in August 2026 [S4]. Incumbent bundling is advancing: Cisco and HPE expose location inside wireless licences, and Quuppa is pushing tag costs toward one to two euros [S4]. Only the third force — accumulated site data — pushes the other way, and it is the one with no evidence behind it [S20, S4]. A narrowing moat is why the base case exits at 9x revenue rather than the 15x-plus a leader in a defended category commands. At 9x on $200M of 2030 revenue the exit is $1.8B, which after 30% dilution returns 1.26x on the $1B entry mark — about 6% a year over four illiquid years [C8]. If the moat holds instead of narrowing, 12x on $500M returns 4.20x [C9]. If standards absorb the capability, the estate sells for patents and team at $400M, returning 0.28x [C7]. The spread between those three is a judgment about durability, not about engineering quality.

text.en: What to check: the split between binding contracts and non-binding memoranda inside the $450M+ aggregate, a named production customer with a contract duration, a signed carrier agreement, and an independent claim-scope review of the patents against 3GPP standard-essential positioning methods. Those four facts would move the grades below more than any further market work could.
The category is large and compounding above 20% a year, but no report sizes the software-only slice ZaiNar actually sells. This dimension scores 9 of 12.
A real technical position in precision positioning, held without a single named production customer to prove buyers choose it. This dimension scores 8 of 15.
The patent estate is the strongest asset in the file, and 3GPP standardization is the thing most likely to make it worth less. This dimension scores 12 of 18.
1. How it makes money

ZaiNar sells software that rides on radios someone else already installed, and it charges for that software four different ways. The independent read of the business describes revenue coming from network software licenses, platform subscriptions, deployment and integration services, and usage-based fees, sold into mobile-network operators, private-5G operators, large enterprises and governments [S4]. The sale runs in three steps: the network is qualified, the customer pays for a pilot, and the pilot becomes a production site license across one or more facilities [S4]. That is a sensible shape for an asset-light infrastructure company — the company buys no tags, no anchors and no beacons, so nothing it sells carries a bill of materials. It is also a slow shape. Qualifying a radio network is telecom engineering work, and a paid pilot is a budget line a hospital or a factory has to defend before the production contract exists.

items.en: The customer pays for a licence, not a device, which is what makes the gross-margin ceiling high in principle. Network software licences and platform subscriptions are the recurring core; deployment and integration services and usage fees sit alongside them [S4]. A licence has almost no unit cost, so on paper this is the asset-light software track, where an infrastructure company should be able to hold gross margin above 75% — gross margin being the share of each revenue dollar left after the cost of delivering the service. The services line is what stands between the model and that number, because integration hours are paid in headcount and do not scale with the licence.

Who signs is an operator or an enterprise, and neither buys quickly. Buyers are mobile-network operators, private-5G operators, large enterprises and governments, reached through network qualification and then a paid pilot [S4]. Carrier relationships may be structured as revenue share rather than a licence [S4], which would trade margin for reach — the carrier sells into its own base and keeps a cut. That is the good version of the standardization threat: if positioning becomes a native network feature but ZaiNar's accuracy still leads, carriers resell the software instead of replacing it.

The strongest disclosed commercial proof is an aggregate, and it is not a customer list. The company reported more than $450M in contracts and memoranda of understanding at its 19 February 2026 launch [S1], restated as more than $500M in the 20 April 2026 Tokyo announcement [S3]. Nine years after founding, not one commercial customer is named in any of it; the only named, dated counterparty anywhere is the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, which selected ZaiNar as one of seven companies from 22 countries for a market-entry support program in April 2026, with no contract value disclosed [S3].

text.en: The aggregate deserves to be argued both ways, because it is the single largest commercial fact on file. The bull reading is straightforward: $450M+ of contracts and memoranda is a very large number for a company of roughly 50-60 people [S4, S8], and enterprises do not sign even non-binding memoranda for technology they have not seen work. The bear reading is equally plain: a memorandum of understanding is a statement that two parties would like to do business, and it carries no obligation to pay. The commercial aggregate is valuable evidence of demand. It is not revenue, and no source anywhere splits the binding contracts from the memoranda [S4]. Until that split exists, the figure sizes interest rather than income.

The $500M+ restatement in April is the same problem one step further on. Between February and April the aggregate rose by roughly $50M, which reads like commercial progress and may well be [S1, S3]. But an increase in a number that mixes signed contracts with letters of intent can come entirely from the non-binding half, so it cannot be read as bookings [S4]. A reader who wants a single sentence on this should take the one that follows. Two disclosures eight weeks apart moved a blended figure up by about a tenth, and neither disclosure said what share of it anyone is contractually obliged to pay.

Alongside the aggregate sits a reported ambition of roughly $5B in pipeline deals, relayed on 20 February 2026, one day after the launch [S18]. That is an internal target, not signed pipeline and not revenue, and it anchors nothing here. The reason to mention it at all is calibration: a company that describes a $5B ambition and a $450M+ aggregate in the same week, while naming no customer, is telling us about its intent rather than its book.

Two channels could change the shape of the sale. The first is the carrier channel, which was described at launch as major carrier and enterprise partnerships to be announced in the coming weeks [S1]; no source confirms a signed one in the seven months to August 2026 [S4]. The second is silicon: ZaiNar joined the Arm Total Design ecosystem for location awareness in physical AI, which puts the capability in front of chip designers [S16]. Neither carries a disclosed contract value. Both remain options on distribution rather than distribution, and without them every enterprise is won one network qualification at a time.
2. The numbers

There is no revenue line to trace. No revenue, ARR (annual recurring revenue — the value of subscription contracts over twelve months) or bookings figure appears in the launch release, the Tokyo announcement, or any press or vendor coverage reviewed [S1, S3, S4]. Preqin, which carries the February 2026 raise, leaves its enterprise-value, revenue-multiple and EBITDA-multiple fields blank for this asset [S9] — a data vendor that sells multiples has none to sell here. The ~$24M ARR and +180% growth that appear in our own registry are self-labelled placeholders from a June 2026 design mock with no document behind them; they are excluded from every number here and named only because their absence is the point [S19]. What follows is therefore a picture of what is known and what is missing, with the missing items stated as what they cost us.

text.en: Read together, these rows cut badly for the investment. Every line that would tell us whether the business works is empty, and the one line that is full — the $450M+ to $500M+ aggregate — is the line whose composition is undisclosed [S1, S3, S4]. That is not a neutral gap. A company nine years old, seven months past a public launch, carrying a $1B+ mark, has published no figure that a buyer could divide into that mark. The $200M of 2030 revenue in the base case is ours, built to see what the price needs rather than derived from anything the company has said [C8].

items.en: Growth cannot be measured, because there are no two points to measure between. A growth rate needs a prior-period figure and a current one, and neither exists in any source [S4, S9]. The commercial aggregate rising from $450M+ in February 2026 to $500M+ in April 2026 is the only movement on file [S1, S3], and it is movement in a blended number, so it establishes activity rather than growth.

Retention is unknown because there is no disclosed installed base to retain. Net dollar retention — how much last year's customers spend this year, as a percentage — is the single most informative metric for a software infrastructure company, and above 130% is what a premium price normally requires. No customer count, renewal, upsell or churn figure appears anywhere [S4]. With no named production account seven months after launch [S4], there is not yet a cohort old enough to have renewed.

Unit economics are absent on both sides of the ledger: no price per site and no cost to serve. Sales-cycle length, average contract value and implementation time per site are all undisclosed [S4], so customer acquisition cost and its payback period cannot be constructed. For a sale that runs network qualification, then a paid pilot, then a production licence [S4], the payback period is the number that decides whether growth is limited by demand or by cash.

Cash is the one place the position looks comfortable, and even there the figure is rounded. The company raised $100M+ in February 2026 [S1], roughly 85% of the approximately $117M raised across all four rounds since 2018 [C4]. Against a headcount of about 50-60 [S4, S8], a raise of that size is several years of payroll on any ordinary assumption, so near-term solvency is not the question. Burn, runway and the cash balance itself are undisclosed [S4, S9], so the pace at which that money is being spent is unknown.

Headcount is small relative to what the aggregate would require delivering. About 50-60 people, with Dealroom showing under 100 [S4, S8], carry a $450M+ commercial figure, a Belmont headquarters and a Tokyo office opened in April 2026 [S3]. No source discloses deployment-team size or time-to-go-live per site [S4]. If the binding share of the aggregate is large, the delivery capacity to recognize it is not visible; if the binding share is small, the headcount fits — and both readings cannot be comforting at once.

An integration-heavy telecom sale genuinely is slow, and a vendor mid-qualification with a carrier often cannot name the account. Sequencing explains part of the silence. It does not explain all of it: a company can disclose the binding share of its own backlog, a gross margin or a revenue figure without naming a single customer, and none of those has been published either [S4, S9]. Absence of disclosure is information, and here it points at an early book rather than a concealed one.
3. Healthier or hungrier

text.en: Hungrier — the company is funding its commercial proof rather than being funded by it. Roughly 85% of the approximately $117M raised since 2018 arrived in the single February 2026 round [C4], which means eight of the company's nine years were spent on about $17M and the business is only now paying for scale. The price attached to that moment tells the same story from the other side: the $1B+ mark divided by revenue is undefined because no revenue is disclosed, and the only ratio available — $1,000M ÷ $450M = 2.2x the blended contracts-and-memoranda figure — measures the quality of a disclosure rather than the value of a business [C3]. A healthy late-stage software company raises against a revenue base that is visible to the buyer. ZaiNar is raising against an aggregate whose binding share has never been published, so it is hungrier, not healthier.

That verdict is not the same as saying the company is in trouble. Cash is almost certainly not the near-term constraint: $100M+ landed in February 2026 [S1] against a headcount of about 50-60 [S4, S8], which on any ordinary payroll assumption funds several years. The constraint is proof. The money buys time to convert a pipeline, and the conversion is the thing no one outside the company can see.

text.en: The bridge reads as a sequence of open steps, and the first one is the cheapest to close and the most consequential. Splitting the $450M+ into binding and non-binding requires no new customer and no new technology — it requires a schedule the company already holds. Until it appears, the same figure supports the base case, in which a modest share converts into production licences and 2030 revenue reaches $200M at a 9x multiple for a 1.26x return, about 6% a year [C8], and the bear case, in which most of the aggregate lapses and a trade sale for the patents and the team returns 0.28x [C7]. One disclosure decides which. That is an uncomfortable amount of the investment's outcome sitting on a document nobody outside the company has seen.

The margin question resolves the same way — by disclosure rather than by argument. On the asset-light software track the test is gross margin above 75%, because a licence carries almost no cost to deliver. Getting there requires the deployment and integration work described in the sales motion to fall to a small share of contract value as sites repeat [S4]. Nothing published shows where it sits today, and a telecom-grade integration business can run far below that line. The 9x multiple used at exit in the base case is a software-infrastructure assumption, not a figure derived from comparable transactions, because the available comp set spans roughly 0.2x to 36x revenue across LiDAR, RFID and telematics names and settles nothing [C5]. If the true margin is a services margin, that multiple is the wrong one and the base case overstates the outcome [C8].
So: hungrier. The capital arrived before the proof, the proof is one unpublished schedule away, and the price already assumes the schedule says the flattering thing.

On the business model and unit economics, the licensing and subscription structure genuinely fits an asset-light infrastructure company, and the carrier revenue-share option would let it survive a shift to network-native positioning as a reseller rather than a casualty [S4]. Against that, not one economic figure behind the model — price, gross margin, cost to serve, payback — has been disclosed [S4, S9]. This dimension scores 6 of 15.

On revenue growth and quality there is less to weigh, because there is nothing to weigh. No revenue, ARR or bookings figure exists in the public record, and the only movement on file is a blended commercial aggregate whose composition is undisclosed [S1, S3, S4]. Growth quality cannot be judged at all. This dimension scores 4 of 15.
1. What the price assumes

The price is above what the evidence supports, and the reason is simple: there is nothing underneath it to test. A $1B+ post-money on a $100M+ raise was announced on 19 February 2026 [S1]. No revenue, ARR or bookings figure has ever been published, so the usual arithmetic — price divided by revenue — has no denominator at all [S4, S9, C3]. Two methods that would normally settle this question are unavailable here, and that is worth saying once and plainly. A comparable-company multiple cannot be applied, because the only comp set on file spans roughly 0.2x to 36x revenue across LiDAR, RFID and telematics businesses, several of them loss-making — an average across business models that different carries no information [S7, C5]. A discounted cash flow cannot be built either, because no cost structure, gross margin or burn rate exists to discount [S4, S9]. What remains is two priced rounds and the arithmetic of what has to happen for the money to come back.

So the price has to be judged against what the buyer is already paying for. At $1,000M, the only ratio available divides the mark by the commercial aggregate the company disclosed at launch: $1,000M ÷ $450M = 2.2x [C3]. That aggregate is $450M+ of customer contracts and memoranda of understanding — a memorandum of understanding being a written statement of intent that neither side is obliged to honour [S1]. No source splits the binding share from the non-binding share, and no customer inside it is named [S4]. A ratio built on that figure measures the quality of a disclosure, not the value of a business. Put the same point in cash terms: the buyer at $1,000M pays about $550M above the last corroborated priced mark [C1], and the assets that have visibly arrived since then are $100M+ of new cash and a patent estate the company reports as 100+ filings and 90+ issued [S1]. Everything else in the price is the expectation that the aggregate converts.

items.en: ZaiNar against its own last priced mark: the step-up is ordinary, not exceptional. $1,000M ÷ $579.37M = 1.73x over roughly 4.4 years, which compounds at 1.73^(1/4.4) − 1 = 12.9%, about 13% a year [C1]. The Series A closed on 31 August 2021 at $23.09 per share on $11.71M raised, and Tracxn independently shows the same ~$579M post-money, so this is the one mark in the file that two sources agree on [S5, S6]. Thirteen percent a year is the return profile of a decent credit fund, earned inside a venture-risk asset. One aggregator chart frames the company as a 64x-from-seed story by skipping this interim mark entirely [S7]; the interim mark is the one that matters, because it is the one a buyer today is stepping up from.

ZaiNar against the listed and private comp set: no usable read, and the dispersion is the finding. The aggregator comp table runs from roughly 0.2x to 36x revenue [S7, C5], and Preqin's enterprise-value, revenue-multiple and EBITDA-multiple fields for this asset are all blank [S9]. A blank field at a paid institutional data vendor is evidence in itself: no independent party has computed a multiple for this name, because there is no revenue line to compute one from. That is why the exit multiples used later — 9x in the base case, 12x in the bull — are stated as assumptions about what software infrastructure fetches, not as numbers derived from any comp table [C5].

ZaiNar against what infrastructure software normally earns: the calibration is ours, and it is where the 9x comes from. Listed infrastructure-software leaders have generally changed hands in a band of roughly 10-20x forward recurring revenue, with the upper half reserved for companies showing net revenue retention above 130% — how much last year's customers spend this year, as a percentage. ZaiNar discloses no recurring revenue and no retention figure of any kind [S4], so the lower end of that band, discounted for an integration-heavy telecom sales motion, is the honest place to sit: 9x in the base case [C8]. A reader new to this should take the point that 9x is not a punitive assumption. It is the modest end of a range this company has not yet earned the right to be measured against.

text.en: Read together, those rows cut against the investment. The two rows carrying real evidentiary weight are both round marks, and the more recent of the two is the company's own rounded number. Every row that would let a buyer test the price against operating performance is empty. That does not make the company weak; it makes the price untestable, and an untestable price at $1B+ is a worse bargain than a high multiple on a disclosed number, because a high multiple can at least be argued down with facts.

One more figure belongs here for scale. Cumulative capital raised is about $117M: $2M and $3M seeds in 2018, roughly $12M in the 2021 Series A, and $100M in February 2026 [S7, C4]. Roughly 85% of every dollar this company has ever raised arrived in the last round. The business as it exists today has therefore been funded for about seven months at scale, and the $1B+ mark prices nine years of stealth research plus seven months of commercial operation. That is what the entry price already assumes.
2. Fair value & scenarios

Fair value range: $0.6B - $1.3B. Priced-round precedent only. No revenue figure exists to multiply, and no discounted cash flow can be built without a cost structure or burn rate [S4, S9]. The low end is the corroborated August 2021 Series A post-money of $579.37M [S5, S6]; the high end adds 30% to the February 2026 $1B+ mark for the $100M+ of new cash and the issued patent estate [C2].

The band is wide on purpose, and the width is the message. It rests on two round marks and nothing else: $579.37M ≈ $0.6B at the bottom, and $1,000M × 1.30 = $1.3B at the top [C2]. A range that spans more than a factor of two is not a precise answer, and no amount of method would narrow it — only disclosure would. The entry mark of $1B+ sits in the upper quarter of that band [S1]. A buyer at that level is paying near the top of a range whose top was set by adding an assumed 30% uplift to the company's own rounded number. That is the structural problem with this price in one sentence.

The three cases below all run from the same $1,000M entry to a 2030 exit, four years of holding, with 30% dilution assumed between now and then — meaning a holder's stake is reduced by later financing rounds, so only 70% of the exit value accrues to money invested today [C7, C8, C9]. They differ in one variable that matters: whether the commercial aggregate becomes revenue, and whether standardized network positioning lets anyone charge for it.

items.en: Bear — the technology works and the business does not, returning 0.28x. 3GPP Release 18/19 and RAN-native positioning absorb the capability, most of the $450M+ aggregate lapses as memoranda that never convert, and the company sells to a network incumbent for its patents and team below the last private mark. Exit year 2030. Exit revenue: not disclosed — this case has no revenue line, because the exit is priced on assets rather than earnings, so no exit multiple applies (n/a). Exit value $400M; $400M × 0.70 = $280M; $280M ÷ $1,000M = 0.28x gross MOIC — money returned divided by money invested — which is an IRR of −27% a year across four years [C7]. Roughly three quarters of the money is lost even though the engineering is sound. The patent estate is what stops this going to zero.

Base — it sells, and the entry price still eats the return: 1.26x. The company converts a modest share of the contracts-and-MOU aggregate into production site licenses across healthcare and industrial sites, signs no transformative carrier deal, and exits at a software-infrastructure multiple on real but sub-scale revenue. Exit year 2030; exit revenue $200M; exit multiple 9x. 9 × $200M = $1.8B exit value; $1.8B × 0.70 = $1.26B; $1.26B ÷ $1,000M = 1.26x gross MOIC, an IRR of 6% a year [C8]. Six percent a year, with the capital locked up and unmarkable for four years, is the reward for the company executing its plan. The entry mark, not the execution, is what caps this.

Bull — the carrier channel signs and the accuracy gap survives, returning 4.20x. A named carrier partnership lands, the accuracy gap over standardized RAN positioning holds, and accumulated site data becomes the switching cost the company claims, making ZaiNar the default positioning layer for physical AI deployments. Exit year 2030; exit revenue $500M; exit multiple 12x. 12 × $500M = $6.0B exit value; $6.0B × 0.70 = $4.2B; $4.2B ÷ $1,000M = 4.20x gross MOIC, an IRR of 43% a year [C9]. This case pays properly. It needs two independent things to land, and neither has landed in the seven months since the February 2026 launch [S1, S4].
